name: Treadle lathe with flywheel
note: The flywheel stores kinetic energy from foot pedal, giving continuous cutting rather than reciprocating bow drive. One person can now hold and feed work. Enables cam operation and steady-speed cutting.

name: Mandrel and self-centering chuck
note: The mandrel supports rotating spindles; the chuck holds work concentrically. Requires conical taper fitting and 1mm hand-scraped seating. Enables repeatable centering without re-marking.

name: Lathe faceplate and driving plates
note: Cast-iron plate bolts to spindle nose; work bolts to plate. Hand-scraped face ensures coplanarity to 1mm. Without it, work runout is uncontrolled. Enables chucking of large irregular work.

name: Tailstock and dead centre
note: Tailstock slides along bed and clamped in position; dead centre (hardened point) supports work end without rotation. Conical fit and hand-scraped fit require cap_tol_1mm. Axial runout then limited by lathe spindle.

name: Simple slide rest on lathe bed
note: Carriage slides on bed Ways are hand-scraped flat and parallel to 1mm. Lead screw (from master_screw) drives longitudinal feed. Tool holder is hand-clamped on cross-slide. Now a human can feed accurately without constant hand-jiggling. Enables repeatable diameters to 1mm.

name: Compound slide rest with two lead screws
note: Cross-slide mounted on top of longitudinal slide, also driven by lead screw. Enables angled cuts and conical threads. Compound angle reduces tangential cutting error. Requires two independent lead screws or gebraic linkage, both needing cap_tol_100um threads.

name: Back-gear reduction drive
note: Gear train engaged by clutch reverses spindle direction and reduces speed 3:1 to 5:1. Allows heavy roughing and soft brasses without exceeding foot speed. Teeth cut by hand with gear cutter or master cutter. Enables slow steady feeds on long work.

name: Change gears and quadrant for automatic feed
note: Interchangeable gear pairs couple spindle to lead screw. Quadrant index positions gears. Swapping gears changes feed rate and thread pitch. Gear ratios must maintain thread lead precision, so gears need cutting accuracy 0.1mm pitch. Eliminates hand-wheel cranking.

name: Capstan and turret lathe
note: Turret holds 6-8 tools indexed by hand. Capstan (large handwheel) feeds work to preset stops. Repeatable positioning requires mechanical stops accurate to 0.1mm. Unskilled operator can repeat production. Massive labour saving, hence state interest.

name: Automatic screw machine with cams and limit stops
note: Driven by steam motor. Cams and trip dogs sequence tool operations and advance work. Completely unattended running once set. Operator knowledge needed is minimal: just threading the magazine. Scares artisans. Requires skilled cam grinder and cap_tol_100um stops.

name: Planing machine (bed and tool)
note: Tool holder reciprocates on massive rigid base. Work bolted to moving table under tool. Cast-iron bed hand-scraped for parallelism and flatness to 1mm over metre length. Much heavier than lathe, needs water power. Now surfaces can be finished flat. Gap: no vertical motion yet.

name: Shaper machine with quick-return mechanism
note: Crank-driven tool bar moves in short stroke, cutting on extension only. Quick-return allows work positioning during return. Whitworth linkage or Hydraulic feed enables vertical and horizontal capability on same machine. Smaller footprint than planer, hence more popular. Enables T-slots and pockets.

name: Slotter machine for keyways and slots
note: Vertical tool bar reciprocates. Rotary table beneath allows indexing work for slots and keyways. Precision of slot depth depends on stop blocks accurate to 0.1mm. Enables gearbox internals and shaft-coupling slots. More specialised than shaper.

name: Milling machine with rotating cutter
note: Rotating multi-flute cutter cuts on peripheral edges and end. Perpendicular feed removes vastly more material than planing. Requires spindle bearings accurate to 0.1mm runout and feed screws with matching tolerance. The spindle-bearing precision is the hard part.

name: Fly cutter for large flat faces
note: Single cutting tool offset on rotating radius. Covers large area with single spiral pass. Slow but saves time on facing big castings. Tip must be brazed and ground to 0.1mm flatness. Enables facing of casting parting surfaces.

name: Universal milling machine with tilting head and swivel table
note: Spindle tilts horizontally and vertically. Table swivels to any angle. Can mill helical flutes and angled teeth. Requires precision indexing to 0.1 degrees and feed positioning to 0.1mm. More versatile, hence more skilled operator required.

name: Dividing head for indexing and spiral milling
note: Spindle indexed via worm gear (ratio 40:1). Index plate with holes and sector arms set the angle. Enables cutting gears, cams, and helical grooves. Accuracy depends on worm gear backlash (must be <0.05mm at spindle) and hole spacing precision (0.1mm).

name: Surface grinder with reciprocating electromagnet
note: Rotating abrasive wheel at 1500-3000 rpm feeds into work on moving table. Electromagnet holds ferrous work. Enables finish to 0.01mm (10 microns). Wheel must be balanced and trued, else vibration ruins finish. Requires cap_tol_10um table motion.

name: Cylindrical grinder for external and internal
note: Work spindle rotates; abrasive wheel feeds radially. Wheel can work OD, ID, or both. Requires cap_tol_10um spindle bearings and table feed. Enables bearing journals and piston fit bores to 10 microns.

name: Tool and cutter grinder for milling tool angles
note: Grinding wheel at multiple indexable angles grinds rake, relief, lip, and spiral angles into milling tools. Requires angle measurement to 0.5 degrees and radial feed to 0.01mm. Masters the milling industry.

name: Jig boring machine with precision spindle
note: Spindle runout <0.002 inches (50 microns) via precision bearings. Quill feed screw cuts jig holes to 0.01mm location in cast castings. Dial indicator on spindle measures hole position to 0.01mm. Enables mass production of interchangeable jigs and tooling.

name: Honing machine for cylinder bores
note: Multiple small honing stones in rotating mandrel cut on expansion, removing 0.002 to 0.005 inch (50-125 micron) from bore. Produces 0.5 micron finish and 0.01mm roundness. Critical for engine cylinders and hydraulic actuators.

name: Lapping with cast-iron plate and abrasive compound
note: Emery and oil rubbed on massive cast-iron plate removes 1-10 microns and polishes to 0.5 micron finish. Flat lapping generates three-plate flatness automatically. Slow: 1mm removal per hour. Essential after grinding to remove burr and achieve optical quality.

name: Drill press with feed screw and depth stop
note: Spindle rotates on precision bearings. Feed screw lowers drill into work at controlled rate. Stop blocks set depth repeatably to 1mm. Eliminates hand-pressure variation and dangerous walk. Enables accurate hole spacing in jigs.

name: Twist drill with helical flute
note: Helical flute evacutes chips from deep holes. Two-flute geometry creates cutting edges and flute valleys. Requires precise grind of point angle and lip relief. Invention is the flute clearance geometry, not the point. Enables deep, clean drilling.

name: Taps and dies with thread standards
note: Whitworth thread (55-degree, interchangeable with sizes) costs little to standardize. Hand tap cuts internal thread; die cuts external. Both must be hard (hardened steel 50 Rc+) and accurate 0.05mm pitch. Huge cost benefit: parts interchangeable, no custom threads per customer.

name: Reamer with multiple flutes
note: Four or six flutes; cutting edges at same diameter. Removes 0.05mm per side per pass. Produces finish accurate to 0.1mm on ID. Used after drill to reach tolerance. Machine reamer with back-taper prevents binding.

name: Broach tool and broaching machine
note: Long bar with progressive teeth (each 0.1mm taller) pulled or pushed through hole or across surface. Removes complex profile in one stroke. Requires 0.05mm tooth accuracy and strong machine frame. Enables keyways, splines, and precision slots.

name: Arbor press for bearing and gear installation
note: Screw-driven ram applies steady pressure (up to 5 tonnes). Arbors (hardened tapers) support work true to mandrel. Enables interference fits (bearing on shaft) and gear assembly without hammer risk. Repeatability to 1mm.

name: Hand-scraped surface plate and why it beats grinding
note: Scraper removes 0.002-inch (50 micron) peaks by hand, leaving high spots touching across area. Flatness reaches 0.05mm over metre. Grinding the same size plate requires weeks; hand scraping requires weeks but leaves damping-friendly rough surface. Machine slides run smoother and quieter on scraped surfaces.

name: Straightedge and reference straightness
note: Cast-iron bar hand-scraped flat within 0.05mm over metre length. Light falls through 0.1mm gap if not in contact. Essential reference tool. Worn straightedges become rounded and measure optimistically: must be checked against other straightedges in rotation.

name: Reference square derived from plane
note: Plane sole determines angle to 0.05 degrees via scraping. Steel blade face and stem form square's working edge. Tested by rotation on surface plate: blade and plate contact all around. Enables perpendicularity checking.

name: Cylindrical square for checking bores
note: Cylinder ground to 0.01mm runout. Inserted into bore; any deviation from perpendicularity shows as rocking. Enables checking cylinder squareness to axis at 0.1mm per metre. Precision depends on grind quality.

name: Sine bar and sine plate for angle measurement
note: Steel bar with two precision cylinders at known distance (5 or 10 inches). Tilting it onto gauge blocks sets angle via simple trigonometry. Enables angle grinding and gear pitch to 0.1 degrees. Accuracy requires gauge blocks.

name: Vernier caliper with 0.05mm resolution
note: Sliding scale with 20 divisions over 19mm creates vernier effect: 1mm / 20 = 0.05mm readability. Requires master_screw precision on main scale and fine tooling on slave scale. Hand-readability plateaus at 0.05mm.

name: Depth gauge with vernier for holes and recesses
note: Vernier scale mounted on sliding rod. Parallel base sits on part surface, rod projects down into recess. Measures depth to 0.05mm. Enables depth control in drilling and recessing operations.

name: Dial indicator with 0.01mm resolution
note: Plunger moves gear-driven pointer over dial. 10 mm plunge motion maps to 100 mm dial rotation, enabling 0.01mm readability. Mechanical magnification via gearing. Enables spindle runout and table flatness checking.

name: Optical comparator for part profiling
note: Overhead lens projects magnified silhouette (30x to 100x) onto screen. Operator aligns part edge to master outline. Enables rapid profile checking and sorting of gears, cams, and punch dies. Fast but less accurate than dial indicator.

name: Gauge blocks and wringing with 0.5 micron accuracy
note: Hardened steel blocks ground to 0.5 micron accuracy. Wringing (sliding together under pressure) removes air film, blocks stick by molecular force. Stacking 5-6 blocks builds any length. Enables checking micrometer accuracy and jig boring positions. Game-changer for interchangeable manufacturing.

name: Go-no-go gauges for production sorting
note: Two gauges: 'go' is at tolerance max, 'no-go' at min. Part passes both or is scrapped. Requires gauge block accuracy for calibration. Unskilled worker can sort: one part per second. Cost is high precision gauge cost; labour cost drops to near-zero.

name: Optical flat and Newton's rings for flatness
note: Thick glass plate ground flat within 0.2 microns. Monochromatic light creates Newton's rings: dark fringes show topography to 0.25 microns. Enables checking grinder wheel truing and lapping plate flatness. Only optical method for surface checking under 1 micron.

name: Autocollimator for angle and parallelism measurement
note: Telescope with reticule and light source reflects light off target mirror. Tilt changes reflected spot on reticule. Each 1mm spot shift = 3 arc-seconds tilt. Enables checking machine tool bed parallelism and spindle axis alignment to 1 arc-second.

name: Toolmaker's microscope with precision stage
note: Compound microscope (50x) on XY stage with lead screws and vernier scales. Stage moves 0.01mm per vernier division. Enables measuring tool angles, pitch dimensions, and edge geometry. Combined with optical flat, verifies tool geometry to 1 micron.

name: Profile projector for large-scale part checking
note: Lens projects magnified shadow (50x to 200x) onto screen. Part mounted on XY stage accurate to 0.01mm. Operator aligns part against master profile drawn on screen. Faster than toolmaker's microscope for large parts, less accurate.

name: Three-wire method for screw thread pitch diameter
note: Three hardened cylinders positioned in thread grooves (two on bottom, one on top). Vernier measures distance across wires. Simple algebra (lookup table) converts to pitch diameter. More robust than pitch micrometer. Enables Whitworth thread verification.

name: Roundness measurement without perfect reference
note: Part rotates on spindle (10 micron runout max). Dial indicator holds tip against surface as part turns. Mechanical filter (averaging arm) removes spindle runout, reading only part roundness error. Requires knowledge that runout and roundness are separable.

name: Climate-controlled metrology room at 20 Celsius
note: 20 Celsius is reference; 1 degree change changes steel 0.01mm per metre. Granite surface plates on massive piers isolate from vibration. Ventilation removes body heat and light heat. Expensive, rare, but essential for 0.01mm accuracy. Most toolrooms ignore it, achieving 0.1mm instead.

name: Standard metre and wavelength of light standard
note: Platinum standard metre bar defines length. Later: wavelength of red Cd light = 643.847 nm = definition of metre. Moves definition from object to phenomenon. Enables every lab to define length without artifact reference. Changes metrology from physics-of-things to physics-of-light.

name: Ball and roller bearing with precision grinding
note: Spheres or cylinders ground to 1 micron roundness require automated grinding. Races (inner/outer rings) ground to 10 micron form. Preload and clearance adjusted to limit axial play to 5 microns. Enables spindle speeds 5000+ rpm at 10 micron runout.

name: Ballscrew with recirculating balls and 0.01mm backlash
note: Balls recirculate in helical groove, not sliding friction. Backlash under 0.01mm, no stick-slip. Thread ground to 0.05mm accuracy; ball-raceway hardness (Rc 58+) matches bearing races. Five-fold speed increase and zero runout drift compared to lead screw.

name: Lead screw error correction cam and follower
note: Grinding a lead screw leaves periodic runout (0.05mm). Measuring runout and grinding a cam follower that compensates enables 0.01mm lead accuracy. Follower attached to tool post cancels runout. Expensive, rarely done. Enables perfect pitch on long lead screws.

name: Jig and fixture for interchangeable manufacture
note: Jig: guides drill to accuracy. Fixture: clamps part to machine table concentrically. Both require 0.01mm bore and datum alignment. Jigs for gun parts (musket locks) were state-of-art 1815. Enables unskilled labour to make parts to spec.

name: Toolroom as institution and knowledge centre
note: Dedicated space for gauge making, jig design, machine maintenance. Master machinist leads apprentices. Teaches measurement, geometry, material properties. Institutional memory prevents tool designs being reinvented per factory. Concentrates capital in gauges rather than machinery.

name: Apprentice system and skill transfer in toolmaking
note: Boy apprenticed at 12, bound for 7 years. Learns by doing under master guidance. Picks up tacit knowledge (feel for scraper, reading dial indicator) that cannot be written down. Replaces each master with successor. Lineal transfer of craft.

name: Tool steel, high speed steel, carbide and cutting speed gains
note: Tool steel (plain carbon): 20 m/min on cast iron. HSS (W, V, Cr, Co): 40 m/min, withstands red hardness. Carbide (WC + binder): 200 m/min, but brittle and hard to grind. Each step requires controlled hardening. Carbide demands carbide grinding wheel.

name: Coolant and cutting fluid for speed and finish
note: Sulphurized oil reduces friction 50%, cutting speed 2x. Coolant (water-soluble) prevents thermal expansion error. Turpentine or kerosene for aluminium. Each material has optimal formulation. Enables closer tolerances by heat control.

name: Machine frame and cast iron for damping vibration
note: Grey cast iron: internal friction dampens vibration better than steel. Massive frame (500+ kg) lowers resonant frequency below spindle speed. Chatter (0.01mm ripple at 500 Hz) ruins finish and shortens tool life. Frame design is as important as spindle accuracy.

name: Chatter and self-excited vibration in machine tools
note: Cutting forces excite frame resonance. Tool marks on work regenerate at spindle frequency, reinforcing vibration. Chatter makes 0.1mm ripples, destroying tolerance. Solution: reduce depth-of-cut, increase speed (raises natural frequency), or damp frame. Theoretical explanation late 20th century.

name: Pantograph and copying mechanism for die sinking
note: Stylus follows master template (wood or soft brass). Pantograph linkage (parallelogram with adjustable magnification) drives cutter at 1:1 or scaled. Enables reproducing intricate shapes (gun locks, coin dies). Requires mechanical accuracy to 1mm at scale magnification.

name: Tracer lathe with hydraulic copying
note: Tracing stylus follows master contour. Hydraulic amplifier drives tool cross-feed. Operator controls longitudinal feed manually. Enables conical or curved lathe work (gun barrels, telescope tubes) without manual skill. Reduces labour but requires master casting per variant.

name: Die sinker and electrode erosion
note: Graphite or copper electrode sinks cavity into hardened steel by electrical discharge (arcing in oil). No contact: cuts hardened steel without work-hardening. Enables complex cavities (watch cases, bearing races) without hand scraping. Accuracy 0.1mm; finish poor but suitable for forging dies.
